subject: Critical Thinking
title: Michel Foucault: Power Shapes What Counts as 'Truth'
description: One-minute skill: Michel Foucault: Power Shapes What Counts as 'Truth'.

hook.text: Who decides what's 'sane' & 'insane'? Who defines 'criminal' & 'normal'? Foucault's answer: power does.

buildup.text: Foucault studied how institutions create categories of 'normal' and 'deviant' – and how these categories serve power.

discovery.text: 'Power/knowledge': what counts as 'true' isn't independent of who has power.

twist.text: This doesn't mean truth is just power. It means: always ask WHO benefits from a particular 'truth' being accepted.

climax.text: Foucault's method: genealogy – tracing how 'natural' categories were historically constructed by specific institutions.

punchline.text: Before asking 'Is it true?' ask 'Who decided it's true, & what power does that.

quiz.question: What did Foucault mean by 'power/knowledge'?
options: What counts as 'truth' is shaped by power structures and institutions

details.summary: Michel Foucault argued that truth is not discovered but produced by power structures. What counts as knowledge is determined by institutions, disciplines, and social practices that privilege certain voices and silence others.
details.whyItMatters: Foucault's insight that power and knowledge are inseparable challenges you to ask who benefits from any claim being accepted as true.
takeaways: Knowledge is produced within power structures
Institutions determine what counts as legitimate knowledge
Critical thinking must examine the power behind claims to truth

faq.question: What does Foucault mean by saying power produces knowledge?
faq.answer: Foucault argues that institutions like universities, courts, and hospitals define what counts as knowledge by controlling who can speak authoritatively, what methods are legitimate, and what questions are considered valid.

faq.question: How can Foucault's ideas improve everyday critical thinking?
faq.answer: When you encounter a claim presented as truth, ask: who has the power to make this claim? What institutions support it? Whose perspectives are excluded? These questions reveal the power dynamics behind seemingly neutral facts.
